#9752. How to Survive (Not Thrive) as a Salaryman

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Every generation predicted the death of the middle manager. Every generation was wrong. Now AI is reorganizing firms toward the middle.

Fifteen rules for remaining employed, reasonably sane, and difficult to blame until the train takes you home.

The objective is not promotion. It is not fulfillment. It is not becoming indispensable.

The objective is to remain employed, reasonably sane, and difficult to blame until the train takes you home.

Arriving dramatically early creates expectations. Arriving late creates evidence.

Aim for the narrow zone in which everyone thinks, Yes, he was already here.

You do not necessarily need to work late. You need to understand who notices when you leave.

If your boss is putting on his coat, congratulations: you have suddenly remembered that you also own a coat.

A folder. A laptop. A notebook. Three pieces of paper.

A person walking quickly while carrying a document is almost universally presumed to have somewhere important to be.

The salaryman’s most efficient communication technology.

Someone explains a problem you don’t control: nod.

Someone announces an initiative that will disappear in six months: deeper nod.

Someone asks whether you understand: nod while saying, “Hai.”

Responsibility can theoretically produce promotion.

Blame can definitely produce unemployment.

When receiving an important instruction, create a polite written record of what was decided. You are not building a case against your coworkers. You are ensuring that six months from now nobody discovers that everyone remembers the meeting differently.

Being uniquely useful is also dangerous because nobody will ever let you go home.

The ideal salaryman occupies the fertile middle:

“It would be inconvenient if Tanaka weren’t here.”

A task that takes everyone three hours but takes you 45 minutes does not create 2 hours and 15 minutes of freedom.

You have discovered one of the fundamental laws of salaried employment.

You cannot defeat rain by becoming angry at clouds.

Attend. Take notes. Say one useful thing. Determine whether anything has actually been assigned to you.

The after-work drinking session is allegedly recreational and occasionally neither.

You don’t have to become the drunkest person in the izakaya. Eat. Participate. Pour drinks when appropriate. Laugh. Learn things.

Most importantly, recognize that the organizational chart becomes unusually honest after the second beer.

The train is not merely transportation. It is the membrane between Corporation You and Actual You.

Music. Manga. Games. Books. Staring into nothingness.

Do not voluntarily convert every commute into additional unpaid work.

A company capable of surviving earthquakes, recessions, executive reorganizations and forty-seven PowerPoint presentations can probably withstand your absence until Tuesday.

A family. Basketball. Gardening. Gundam models. A terrible band. Fishing. A neighborhood bar. An obsessive interest in 16th-century maps.

Anything that allows you to answer “Who are you?” without stating your employer.

Some years you acquire skills. Some years you make money. Some years you encounter an excellent boss. Some years you simply avoid the restructuring.

A 30-year career contains a surprising amount of successfully doing nothing catastrophic.

The presentation can be revised tomorrow.

If everything is always urgent, you are not experiencing urgency. You are experiencing management.

The old salaryman bargain was essentially:

Give us your loyalty and we will give you security.

Modern companies cannot always provide the second half.

If the company stops paying adequately, destroys your health, threatens your family life, or offers neither security nor opportunity, remaining loyal isn’t salaryman stoicism.

Show up.Be useful.Don’t become indispensable.Know who actually makes decisions.Keep receipts.Take the vacation.Catch the train.Go home.Have a life there.Repeat until retirement—or a better offer.

Answer the Salaryman Interview on HackerNoon: 27 questions about middle management, rituals, the company bargain, and AI agents. Your answers become a draft you can submit to HackerNoon for publication. Read the interviews, or explore more at salaryman.tech.

Originally published as Field Notes No. 1 on salaryman.tech.

#9751. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9750. Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies

Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which was developed by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs and Honeygain were reorganized as independent platforms under an umbrella entity called Source, which received $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Update, Nov. 5, 11:07 a.m. ET: In a statement shared post-publication, Oxylabs said that while its system is built so that a device can’t be used as a proxy exit node unless they receive a signal that it has consented, the developer faked these signals.

“We have been conducting regular audits of the applications provided by our partners,” the statement reads. “However, following this incident, we will improve the application and application’s build fingerprinting logic to better detect cases where the SDK is running on an unapproved build of an originally authorized application.”

The statement said Oxylabs has no record of any company called Videostrong Technology Co., but it did find between is suppliers the domain “com.abc[.]nexus,” mentioned in the GTIG report as an external malware loader.

“As soon as we saw that, we suspended the relationship and sent them a formal legal inquiry,” the statement reads. “This supplier accounts for less than 1% of our IP address pool. We had a signed contract with them, they assured our QA team that users had given consent, and we saw the consent flow ourselves.”

Further reading: Plume Security Labs white paper on the XCPE botnet (PDF) Black Lotus Labs writeup on LinkedIn TrendAI’s analysis Synthient’s list of affected devices, broken down by model number

#9749. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain.

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network.

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9748. Debugging macOS LaunchAgent Failures With launchctl and Exit Code 78

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Head of Revenue Operations. Revenue analytics, sales ops, and the SQL behind both. Atlanta.

Every morning at 7:45, a job on my Mac runs a reconciliation and posts the results for the finance team. It's an ordinary LaunchAgent: a plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, a Python script, and a log file.

For three mornings in October, it didn't run.

Nothing told me. There was no error in Slack, because the code that sends errors never started. There was no crash report. And the log file, the first place anyone looks, had nothing new in it, because the job failed before it could write a line.

launchd keeps a record of every job's last exit. Ask for it:

The labels in this post are examples. For a quick look at every job, launchctl list shows the last exit status in its second column.

78 is EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h, a configuration error. My script never exits with 78, and that's the tell: when the exit code is one your program doesn't use, your program probably never ran.

Before launchd starts your program, it does some setup. It opens the files named in StandardOutPath and StandardErrorPath, changes into WorkingDirectory, and finds the executable. If any of that fails, your program never starts, and the job ends with 78.

I wanted to know exactly which mistakes produce it, so I loaded a set of deliberately broken test jobs on macOS 26.6 and read what launchd reported:

Two things surprised me. launchd happily creates a missing log folder, so that's not your problem. And a log file it can't open is fatal. Not a warning and not a quiet fallback: the whole job stops, and the error has nowhere to go.

The worst part of debugging a 7:45 job is the 23-hour feedback loop. You don't need it. Copy the plist, give it a new label, swap the program for something harmless, and tell it to run at load. Everything launchd sets up stays the same, so if the setup is broken, you'll see 78 in two seconds:

/usr/bin/true does nothing and exits 0. If the copy still reports 78, the problem is in the setup, not your code. Fix the plist, rerun the copy, and only then touch the real job. Reload the real one with launchctl bootout and launchctl bootstrap so launchd reads the new version.

Once I'd found one of these, I wanted to check the rest. This script reads every plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents, flags the setups that end in 78, and prints each job's last exit code:

crm-sync is the classic upgrade casualty: Python moved, and the plist still points at the old interpreter. weekly-export is a renamed folder. Both fail silently in exactly the same way mine did, and cash-recon gets flagged before it ever has the chance.

The fix took five minutes. Noticing took three days, because every alert I had lived inside the job, and the job never ran. A job that doesn't start can't report its own failure.

What would have caught it on the first morning is a check that doesn't depend on the job at all: something separate that looks for the job's last success and complains when it's missing. It's the same principle I wrote about in small pipelines fail quietly: watch for the last success, not the last error.

The short version, for every LaunchAgent you rely on:

Your GitHub Actions Cron Job Can Disappear Without Failing

#9747. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9746. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

#9744. Building Data Observability for Banking Pipelines

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Data Engineer specialising in Azure, AWS, Databricks, dbt, and scalable data platforms. Writing about Data Engineering, AI, and cloud architecture.

Loud failures are easy. A job crashes, the scheduler turns red, somebody gets paged, and within the hour there is a chat thread with far too many people in it. Annoying, sure, but the system is at least telling you the truth.

The failure I worry about is the quiet one. Every task shows green. The report lands on time. And one number inside it is wrong, because a feed stopped refreshing three days ago or a join started dropping rows, and nothing in the stack was built to care.

In most industries that is an embarrassing dashboard. In banking it can turn into a regulatory submission, a liquidity figure in front of a risk committee, or a customer statement. The stakes shift quite a lot. So this piece is about silent failures: what they look like, why banks are unusually exposed to them, and a way of building observability that catches them before a report breaks. I should say early that it will not catch everything. I'll come back to what it misses.

I can think of three reasons, though there are probably more.

First, the chains are long. A single regulatory figure, say a liquidity coverage ratio, might pass through a core banking extract, a treasury system, a reference data service, a staging layer, a transformation layer and finally a reporting tool. Each hop belongs to someone else, often with a release calendar nobody downstream has seen.

Second, banks lean heavily on batch. Plenty of critical feeds arrive once a day, and some only once a month. If a daily feed breaks on Tuesday, you might not see the damage until the Friday reconciliation, or the month-end close. A long feedback loop gives bad data plenty of time to travel.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable one, a lot of existing monitoring answers the question "did the job run?" when the question that matters is "is the data right?" Those are different questions. A job can run perfectly and load nothing at all.

None of the following is a real incident from a named bank, but the shapes are familiar to anyone who has worked near a data warehouse.

The stale rate table. An FX rates feed from a market data vendor stops updating after a change on the vendor side. Your pipeline keeps reading the table, which still has plenty of rows, so the job-level check passes. Euro and dollar positions get converted at last Wednesday's rate. Totals look sensible. They just are not true.

The shrinking join. An upstream team changes a code in a product reference table, perhaps a new product type with no mapping yet. An inner join quietly drops everything that no longer matches. Three percent of the loan book disappears from a report. Three percent does not look dramatic on a chart. In a capital calculation, it might be very dramatic.

The drifting distribution. A source system starts defaulting a null field, like days past due, to zero. Row counts are identical. The schema is identical. But the share of loans classed as current jumps overnight, and nobody changed a credit policy.

None of these throws an exception. All of them pass a "job succeeded" check.

I'm a bit wary of the word "observability" because vendors have stretched it until it covers almost anything. The distinction I find useful is simple. Monitoring checks things you already know can go wrong. Observability means collecting enough information about the data itself, continuously, that when something strange happens you can work out where it started and what it touched.

For data, that mostly means watching the data and not only the machinery. CPU on the warehouse tells you very little about whether the FX table is current.

There are lots of ways to slice this. The five below are the ones I keep coming back to, partly because each maps neatly to one of the failures above.

Freshness. When did this table last change, compared with when it should have? One trap here: check the business date inside the data, not the load timestamp. A job can load yesterday's rates today and look perfectly fresh by the wrong clock. That is exactly how the stale rate table slips through.

Volume. Are row counts in a plausible range? The word that matters is plausible, because banks have calendars. UK bank holidays, month-end, quarter-end and year-end all change expected volumes. A check that ignores them will cry wolf every few weeks, and people will stop listening.

Schema. Have columns been added, dropped or retyped? This is the cheapest signal to collect and often the most useful, since a renamed column is a common cause of everything downstream going subtly wrong.

Distribution. Null rates, value ranges, category proportions, and sums of balances. This is where the drifting distribution gets caught. It is also the noisiest signal, so I would introduce it last.

Lineage. Which reports depend on this table? When a check fails, lineage tells you the blast radius. Without it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging" and everyone shrugs. With it, the alert reads "something is odd in staging, and it feeds the liquidity report due at 10am". That is a very different conversation.

Here is the layout I would sketch on a whiteboard. The main idea is that checks live at the boundaries between layers, not only at the end next to the report.

Reading it left to right, the data moves from source systems through ingestion, raw storage, staging, curated marts, and finally the regulatory and management reports. Underneath, an observability layer attaches a different kind of check to each stage.

At ingestion, you ask the cheap questions: did the file arrive, is it fresh by business date, does the schema match the agreed contract? In staging, you look at keys, referential integrity and null rates. In the marts, you run reconciliations and distribution checks. At the report layer, you compare control totals against the prior period and against the general ledger.

Reconciliation deserves a special mention because it is old-fashioned and brilliant. Finance teams have done it for decades. The idea is that the sum of balances in your mart should equal the sum in the source extract, within a tolerance. If a join drops three percent of the loan book, a control total notices immediately, even though row counts and schemas look fine. Plenty of data teams skip it because it feels unglamorous. I would start there.

Every check writes its result to a metadata store. That store feeds the alerting layer and, ideally, a lineage graph, so a failure can be traced to the reports it threatens.

A small example of the volume check, written as plain SQL so it is easy to port. It compares the latest day against the same weekday over the past eight weeks. Treat it as a sketch rather than production code, because it knows nothing about holidays yet.

If the z-score goes past something like 3, raise a flag. The threshold is a guess you will tune, and you should expect to be wrong about it the first few times.

Collecting signals is the easy half. The harder half is making sure a human reacts to them.

I have seen, or at least heard enough war stories to believe in, the pattern where a team switches on two hundred checks, gets forty alerts a day, and within a month has muted the channel. At that point you have built an expensive way of generating noise. So the design question is less "what can we check?" and more "what deserves to interrupt someone?"

A scheme that tends to hold up has three tiers. Informational checks get logged and reviewed weekly. Warnings go to the named owner of the dataset during working hours. Critical failures, meaning anything that touches a regulatory report, go to the owner immediately and also close a gate in front of the publish step.

That gate is the controversial part. Some teams prefer to publish anyway with a visible warning banner, on the argument that a late report is worse than a flagged one. Others hold the previous approved version until someone signs off. I lean towards holding for regulatory outputs and warning for internal dashboards, but I can see the other side. If your submission deadline is fixed by a regulator, the calculation changes.

Whichever way you go, two things matter more than the tooling. Every dataset needs a named owner, a person and not a shared inbox. And upstream teams need a lightweight data contract, even a one-page agreement, saying which columns and codes they promise not to change without notice. Without that, you are monitoring someone else's decisions with no way to influence them.

I would be overselling it if I stopped there.

Observability catches data that is stale, missing, malformed or oddly distributed. It does not catch data that is fresh, complete, consistent and simply wrong because the business logic misreads a rule. A risk weight applied to the wrong asset class will sail through every check described above. That needs code review, testing and domain experts, and no dashboard replaces them.

Thresholds can also create false confidence. A check tuned so loosely that it never fires is worse than no check, because people assume it is protecting them. Anomaly detection tools driven by machine learning can help with tuning, but I am slightly cautious about them in a regulated setting. An auditor can read a rule that says "volume within three standard deviations of the weekday baseline". A black box that quietly adapts its own thresholds is harder to defend.

And then there is the organisational side, which no architecture diagram captures. If upstream teams see your alerts as an accusation and not a courtesy, the checks will be ignored. A bit of diplomacy goes a long way here.

If I were starting on Monday, I would not try to cover the whole warehouse. I would pick one regulatory report, trace its lineage back to the ten or so tables it truly depends on, and add three things: freshness by business date, a volume check with a calendar, and a control total that reconciles to source.

Then I would assign owners and run everything in warn-only mode for two weeks. That gives you a feel for false positives before anyone is woken up at night. Only after that would I switch the critical checks to blocking.

That staged approach is slower than a big-bang rollout, and some teams will find it frustrating. But it builds trust in the alerts, and trust is the thing that decides whether anyone responds when the real one fires.

Silent failures are hard because they look like success. The pipeline is green, the report is on time, and the number is wrong. Catching them means shifting attention from whether the job ran to whether the data still makes sense, and doing it at every boundary, not just at the finish line.

None of this is exotic. Freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage, plus a few reconciliations that finance has trusted for decades. The hard parts are the unglamorous ones: ownership, contracts, tuning thresholds and keeping the noise low enough that people still care. If your team is working through the same problem, I would be curious which of the five signals you found most useful in practice. My bet is freshness by business date, but I could easily be wrong.

#9743. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9742. Atlarix 15.13: Sessions That Answer Each Other, and Questions With Real Options

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at atlarix.dev • Fully Autonomous

Atlarix 15.13 is about sessions that work together without you relaying messages between them, and about the moments an agent has to stop and ask you something. Here is what changed, and why each change was needed.

In 15.12, a message sent to a session that was sitting idle waited for you to type something there. The sender saw "waiting", even when nothing was running on the other side. Now, in the desktop app and the CLI, a plain message starts a turn in an idle session, the way a teammate picks up a ping. In editors (VS Code, Zed) and the Chrome panel it is read with your next prompt there. Two things deliberately do not wake anyone: a "that turn ended" notice, which is marked as a notice and needs no answer, and a session you stopped yourself. If you pressed stop, a message waits for you rather than restarting the work you just halted.

A message from another session used to arrive as a folded row with no text, so on your screen it looked blank. Now every surface shows who sent it and the start of what they said: Message from (): . The full text is one keypress or click away: ctrl+o in the CLI, a click in the desktop app and the Chrome panel, Show all in VS Code, and the step's body in ACP editors such as Zed (its title carries the start). In the CLI, the sending side's row names the receiver instead of a session id. We also fixed the CLI bug behind the blank rows: a long transcript stuck to its top, so a turn that arrived without a keypress ran and was saved but never came into view.

When a session needs approval for a command or an edit, another session can now see exactly what it wants to do. list_sessions with pending_of shows the command or the diff. The reviewer then answers it: approve, ask for a change, or reject. Plans work the same way. High-risk requests, such as a command that deletes files, uses sudo or installs software, still go to you and never to a peer. Use it for a lead session that reviews its workers, or for a second model checking the first one's commands before they run.

When the agent needs a decision, ask_user now works like Claude Code's question tool. Each option can carry a one-line description and a Recommended mark. A question can carry a short topic chip and can allow several picks. You can still type your own answer. It has its own card in the desktop app, the CLI, VS Code and the Chrome panel; other ACP editors such as Zed show it as a list you answer by typing. The agent receives your picks as plain text, for example "Lint, Types, a11y audit".

While a turn runs, Enter steers it at its next step and Tab queues a message for after it. New in 15.13: ctrl+s stops the turn and sends everything you queued as one message. Esc is a plain stop, and anything you had queued comes back into your input box, images included, so nothing is sent behind your back or lost. The terminal bell also rings when a turn finishes or needs you.

Three changes target the same cost: re-sending a long conversation the provider has already seen. On Claude models, the main conversation keeps a one-hour prompt cache on its history, not only on its instructions. Things that change every turn (the active plan, finished background work, attachment notes) now travel in the per-turn tail instead of the cached header, so they no longer invalidate it. And a long conversation left idle until just before its cache would expire is compacted then, so coming back does not mean re-sending everything at full price. You can turn that off with ATLARIX_IDLE_COMPACTION=off.

We audited what Atlarix tells its own models and removed the claims the code did not back up: a search tool described as "relevance-ranked" when it is plain ripgrep, a context reminder that reported a different number from the one that triggered it, and memory-writing rules sent to modes that cannot write notes. A model that is told something false about its tools makes worse choices with them.

15.13 also fixes Windows sign-in for the CLI and editors: without the desktop app installed, they used to forget it and ask again. The desktop app and the CLI update themselves to 15.13 (a Linux .deb or .rpm takes the new package from the downloads page). The full list is in the changelog.

Can one Atlarix session approve another session's commands?

Yes. In 15.13 a session can see another's pending request with list_sessions pending_of, then approve, change or reject it. High-risk requests still need the user.

Does a message to an idle Atlarix session start work there?

Yes, in the desktop app and the CLI. A plain message starts a turn in an idle session there; editors and the Chrome panel read it with your next prompt. A turn-ended notice never wakes a session, and neither does a message to a session the user stopped.

How do I send a queued message right away in the Atlarix CLI?

Press ctrl+s. It stops the running turn and sends everything you queued as one message. Esc stops without sending, and puts the queued text back in the box.

#9741. StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents

We’re introducing StateBench, a benchmark for long-context state tracking—how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve.

State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack.

Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds.

To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer.

StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations:

These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives.

To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes.

We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels.

We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length.

When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats.

We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable.

All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong.

Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model.

We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length.

The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments. Transformers learned the easier levels but degraded on longer sequences, and they never learned general finite problems. On the hardest level, the Gated DeltaNet variant with a more flexible memory update generalized the farthest, staying near perfect out to roughly 10 times the length of the longest sequences it saw during training.

For Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models, the gap points to training rather than architecture; trained directly, they learned to handle state-tracking levels their pretrained counterparts couldn’t. Transformers were different—even trained directly, they could never learn the hardest level.

Some questions remain open. Our new proof shows that Gated DeltaNet with a more limited memory update (non-negative eigenvalues) can solve all aperiodic tasks and certain periodic tasks, such as tracking whether a repeated input has occurred an even or odd number of times, under the paper’s fixed-precision arithmetic with rounding. Its exact placement in the hierarchy remains open, including whether it can solve all soluble tasks and how numerical precision or combining it with attention layers affects its capabilities. StateBench also assumes a fixed number of variables, while real tasks often introduce new entities over time. In a long conversation, for example, new people and objects can appear as it unfolds, and the model has to begin tracking them too. The current framework doesn’t yet cover that setting.

As new flavors of recurrent and hybrid architectures emerge, understanding which kinds of state tracking each can handle could help guide how future systems are developed and trained. We hope StateBench gives researchers a finer-grained way to find where models break down—and to build training and evaluation data for the capabilities that still fall short. More fundamentally, we hope it serves as a North Star for researchers to develop new architectures with more robust state-tracking abilities compared to current models.

#9740. OpenMatter Network Positions Decentralized Computing as an Alternative To Data Centers for AI

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

Melbourne, Florida, November 5th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--OpenMatter Network, a pioneer in decentralized infrastructure for agentic artificial intelligence, is positioning its decentralized computing platform as an alternative to massive, centralized data center development amid growing public opposition to new facilities.

The company says its approach can support continued AI adoption by enabling computing workloads to run across distributed resources rather than relying primarily on large-scale data center infrastructure.

The results of Tuesday's midterm elections have put growing public opposition to massive data center development in the national spotlight. However, according to OpenMatter Network, resistance to new facilities need not signal a slowdown in AI adoption. Instead, it could accelerate the transition to a computing model that reduces dependence on massive, centralized data centers.

“Voters have made it clear that they are increasingly concerned about the enormous energy demands, environmental impact and rising utility costs associated with massive data center development,” said Mike Anderson, CEO of OpenMatter Network. “But the need to deploy agentic AI isn’t going away. Businesses don’t have to choose between advancing AI and addressing these very legitimate concerns. There is another path forward, and OpenMatter is helping make it possible.”

Across the country, communities have expressed concerns about the impact of large-scale facilities on electricity rates, water supplies, local infrastructure and the environment. The election has brought renewed attention to those concerns and the policy choices surrounding new construction.

“The assumption that AI must be built around increasingly massive concentrations of computing power deserves to be challenged,” Anderson continued. “Our decentralized architecture allows computing resources to be distributed across many different locations. That means organizations have another way to move forward with agentic AI as communities and policymakers reconsider the costs and consequences of building more enormous data centers.”

The OpenMatter Network platform is designed to transform widely available computing hardware into usable network resources through its distributed architecture, algorithms and verifiable computing capabilities. By enabling independently owned computing resources to participate in a shared network, OpenMatter is working to make decentralized infrastructure a practical alternative for enterprise AI deployment.

“There’s an enormous amount of computing capacity outside the walls of traditional data centers,” said Renee Davis, co-founder and chief business officer of OpenMatter Network. “Our technology makes it possible to bring those resources together in a verifiable network capable of supporting real-world AI workloads. Rather than concentrating computing power in a relatively small number of massive facilities, we can distribute workloads across existing resources and smaller installations, creating opportunities for a more flexible and potentially more energy-efficient approach to AI infrastructure.”

The decentralized model also offers organizations greater flexibility in where computing resources are located and how they are deployed. This can be particularly valuable for businesses and government institutions seeking greater control over computing infrastructure, including those with requirements for data sovereignty and locally managed resources.

“The question is no longer simply how many more massive data centers we need to build,” Anderson concluded. “It’s how we can deploy the AI capabilities businesses need without imposing unnecessary burdens on the communities where computing resources are located. Tuesday’s election results make that question more urgent than ever. OpenMatter offers a new way forward.”

Headquartered in Florida’s Space Coast, OpenMatter Network is building the Verifiable Trust Layer for Secure Collaboration and AI Agents. Guided by the principle “Don’t Trust Data. Prove It.,” the company’s cryptographically verifiable architecture enables secure collaboration, governed AI behavior and mathematically verifiable execution across untrusted environments. For more information, visit www.openmatter.network.

#9739. Auditing 153 Claude Code & Codex transcripts for #107757 User-Agent and URL email leaks (and filtering 259 noreply@anthropic.com hits)

When anthropics/claude-code#107757 and #55743 hit the front page today (where Claude Code injects oauthAccount.emailAddress from ~/.claude.json into context and models copy that email into outbound User-Agent headers or query strings), I wrote a script to audit what my own coding agents had sent over the network across 153 local Claude Code and Codex CLI transcripts (1,928 deduplicated tool calls).

Once synthetic trailers and loopback requests were separated, the audit caught:

I published the zero-dependency auditor as egressleak (npx egressleak):

To block outbound email and token leaks deterministically without waiting for upstream CLI patches or trusting prompt instructions, run the emit-hook generator mode in npx egressleak. It outputs a zero-dependency Node.js PreToolUse guardrail script (~/.claude/hooks/egress-guard-hook.mjs) that inspects Bash, WebFetch, and WebSearch tool inputs and exits with code 2 if an outbound request includes a real email address in User-Agent, an ?authuser= / ?email= query parameter, or a secret API token (sk-, ghp_, AIza).
