#9738. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

#9736. Run the Fence Before You Ship the Paragraph: An Executable-Example Gate for Model-Drafted Docs

A model may draft the prose of a documentation page, but it may not own the example that proves the prose. That single rule converts doc generation from a trust argument into a build step with an exit code, and it holds even when the drafting model is free, fast, and only loosely supervised. Everything below is a working gate built on that rule: prose is model-draftable, executed code is the evidence, and any example that cannot run becomes a named human's problem.

The failure mode this targets is not bad writing. Documentation pages usually rot at the example rather than the sentence: a flag gets renamed, a response field moves, a command silently starts printing a warning that breaks a copy-paste pipeline. Prose drifts slowly and reads plausibly the whole way down, while a broken fence fails loudly the moment somebody executes it. So the gate asks the cheap, objective question first — does this block still run? — and lets that answer decide how much draft text is allowed to survive.

Write the boundary down as a one-line policy, because models follow explicit scopes far more reliably than implicit ones. The model owns sentences that describe behaviour, rationale, and trade-offs; the human owns every fenced example and every sentence whose only support is a failing fence. This split matters because it maps to different verification costs: prose is reviewed by reading, examples are reviewed by executing.

A page therefore has two artifacts with two owners. The prose artifact can be regenerated as often as you like, and the example artifact changes only when a human accepts a new execution result. Keep that distinction visible in your repo layout, so reviewers never have to guess which part of a diff they are approving.

The gate itself is deliberately boring: walk the docs tree, pull out fenced blocks, run the ones that have a runner, and emit a JSON report. Info strings carry control flags, so a block written as `python noexec is parsed but never executed.

"""tools/fence_gate.py - execute every runnable fence under a docs tree.""" from future import annotations

import json import shutil import subprocess import sys import tempfile from dataclasses import dataclass from pathlib import Path

RUNNERS = { "python": (".py", ["python3", "{file}"]), "py": (".py", ["python3", "{file}"]), "bash": (".sh", ["bash", "{file}"]), "sh": (".sh", ["bash", "{file}"]), "js": (".mjs", ["node", "{file}"]), "javascript": (".mjs", ["node", "{file}"]), }

@dataclass class Fence: doc: str line: int lang: str flags: list[str] body: str status: str = "skipped" # passed | failed | skipped | unowned detail: str = ""

def parse_fences(doc: Path) -> list[Fence]: fences: list[Fence] = [] inside, start, info, body = False, 0, "", [] for lineno, line in enumerate(doc.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines(), start=1): stripped = line.strip() if not inside and stripped.startswith(""): inside, start, info, body = True, lineno, stripped[3:].strip(), [] continue if inside and stripped.startswith(""): words = info.split() lang = words[0].lower() if words else "" fences.append(Fence(str(doc), start, lang, words[1:], "\n".join(body))) inside = False continue if inside: body.append(line) return fences

def run_fence(fence: Fence, timeout: int = 20) -> None: if "noexec" in fence.flags: fence.status, fence.detail = "unowned", "marked noexec: needs a named owner" return runner = RUNNERS.get(fence.lang) if runner is None: fence.status, fence.detail = "skipped", f"no runner for {fence.lang!r}" return suffix, argv_tpl = runner exe = shutil.which(argv_tpl[0]) if exe is None: fence.status, fence.detail = "skipped", f"{argv_tpl[0]} not installed" return with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp: path = Path(tmp) / f"fence{suffix}" path.write_text(fence.body, encoding="utf-8") argv = [exe if a == argv_tpl[0] else a.replace("{file}", str(path)) for a in argv_tpl] try: proc = subprocess.run(argv, cwd=tmp, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=timeout) except subprocess.TimeoutExpired: fence.status, fence.detail = "failed", f"timeout after {timeout}s" return fence.status = "passed" if proc.returncode == 0 else "failed" if proc.returncode != 0: tail = proc.stderr.strip().splitlines() fence.detail = tail[-1][:200] if tail else f"exit {proc.returncode}"

def main(root: str, out: str) -> int: results: list[Fence] = [] for doc in sorted(Path(root).rglob("*.md")): for fence in parse_fences(doc): run_fence(fence) results.append(fence) Path(out).write_text(json.dumps([f.dict for f in results], indent=2), encoding="utf-8") bad = [f for f in results if f.status in {"failed", "unowned"}] for f in bad: print(f"{f.status:8} {f.doc}:{f.line} [{f.lang}] {f.detail}") return 1 if bad else 0

if name == "main": raise SystemExit(main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "docs", sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else "fence-report.json")) `

Run it as python3 tools/fence_gate.py docs fence-report.json. The non-zero exit on failure is the whole point: the gate is a test, not a report you read when convenient. Treat a red gate exactly like a red unit test suite.

Four outcomes are enough to cover real docs, and each one maps to a different owner. Encode the mapping once so nobody relitigates it in review.

The skipped row is where most teams quietly cheat. A missing language runtime is an environment fact, not a documentation fact, so the honest response is to keep the example, label it unverified, and assign a person — not to delete it and pretend the page is fully checked.

Ownership that lives in a shared inbox is ownership that nobody holds. Keep a small map from doc path to a person, and let the gate generate the work items directly from the JSON report.

"guide/install.md": "@avery" "guide/webhooks.md": "@ops-docs" "reference/cli.md": "@avery" default: "@docs-oncall" `

`bash jq -r '.[] | select(.status == "failed" or .status == "unowned") | "- [ ] `\(.doc):\(.line)` [\(.status)] — \(.detail)"' \ fence-report.json > fence-issues.md `

That fence-issues.md is the human queue, and it is intentionally short. A page with nine broken examples produces nine checkboxes with file and line numbers, which is a far better review artifact than a paragraph explaining that the docs "may be slightly outdated".

This is where I actually use MonkeyCode: its free model access handles the prose pass, and the free server option runs the fence sweep on a schedule so drift shows up even when my laptop is closed. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. Availability and limits are operator-supplied and change over time, so verify them against the product's current documentation before you build a pipeline around them.

The drafting prompt gets two inputs — the current page and the fence report — and one hard constraint: it may only describe commands, flags, or output shapes that appear in a passed fence. Anything else must be written as an open question addressed to the owner in owners.yml. In practice the model becomes a rewriter of verified material rather than an author of plausible material, and the questions it emits are often the most useful part of the diff.

Schedule the sweep however your environment already schedules jobs, for example 0 6 * * 1 python3 tools/fence_gate.py docs fence-report.json for a Monday morning pass. If you run it on the free server, the command does not change — only the machine that executes it does, which is exactly what you want from a gate.

The gate only proves that a block exits zero, never that it demonstrates the right thing; a fence can pass while teaching an obsolete workflow. Examples that need credentials, network access, or destructive side effects will either fail or need a sandbox you maintain, and flaky ones will teach your team to ignore red builds. Languages without a cheap local runner produce skipped rows forever unless somebody writes a runner.

Skip this approach if your docs are mostly conceptual, if you have no CI or scheduled jobs to hang it on, or if nobody is willing to be the name in owners.yml. A gate with no owner is just a slower way to generate unflagged warnings. Start with one high-traffic page, run the gate for two weeks, and only then decide whether the prose pass is worth automating across the tree.

If you try it, the smallest useful version is Step 2 plus a single owner entry — that combination already tells you which half of your documentation is actually verified.

#9735. Gate Pioneers Proof of Security, Achieving 104.58% Cold Storage Coverage to Solidify Asset Security

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

We're your all-in-one marketing hub tailored for the crypto and blockchain sectors.

Gate has officially introduced Proof of Security (PoSEC), a new asset security verification framework, becoming the first digital asset trading platform in the industry to launch a PoSEC security verification system. Since its founding in 2013, Gate has consistently placed user asset security at the forefront of its priorities.

With the introduction of PoSEC, Gate extends security verification beyond reserve adequacy to include asset storage structures and risk coverage capabilities, further solidifying safeguards for user assets and providing a new practical approach to advancing industry security standards.

Unlike Proof of Reserves (PoR), which primarily verifies the adequacy of asset reserves, PoSEC places additional emphasis on asset storage security. By publicly disclosing the distribution of assets between platform cold storage and hot wallets, PoSEC provides visibility into asset storage structures and their ability to cover potential losses under extreme scenarios.

PoSEC introduces the cold storage coverage ratio as a key metric to measure the extent to which cold storage covers total user assets. A coverage ratio ≥ 100% means that, under the applicable calculation methodology, cold storage alone would be sufficient to cover all user assets even if all assets held in hot wallets were lost. PoR and PoSEC serve complementary purposes, extending asset security verification from reserve adequacy to storage security and risk coverage, while providing users with more comprehensive and transparent information about asset security.

According to the snapshot taken at 00:00 (UTC) on November 4, 2026, Gate's cold storage coverage ratio reached 104.58%, with cold storage and hot wallet assets accounting for 88.26% and 11.74% of total assets, respectively. Cold storage assets include digital assets held offline and traditional assets under independent custody. To qualify, these assets must meet requirements such as not being directly used for routine deposits and withdrawals, being held offline or under independent custody, requiring multi-party authorization for transfers, and being independently verifiable.

The current data is undergoing verification by an independent third-party audit firm. The review covers asset authenticity and control, valuation and calculation methodologies, and coverage ratio calculations. The audit report will be published on Gate's official website upon completion, enhancing the transparency and credibility of asset security disclosures.

Gate has long been committed to digital asset security and transparency. In 2020, Gate was among the first in the industry to introduce an open-source Proof of Reserves (PoR) mechanism and a Merkle Tree-based asset verification solution, establishing itself as an early contributor to reserve transparency in the industry. Gate subsequently incorporated technologies such as zk-SNARKs to enhance its asset reserve verification framework.

As of October 18, 2026, Gate's total reserves amounted to approximately $8.688 billion, with an overall reserve ratio of 118.49%. The platform also employs a range of security mechanisms, including hot and cold wallet segregation, multi-signature technology, Multi-Party Computation (MPC), dynamic risk monitoring, and zero-trust access control, to establish a multi-layered security framework covering asset reserves, storage management, and risk protection.

From PoR, which verifies reserve adequacy, to PoSEC, which verifies asset storage security and risk coverage capabilities, Gate is progressively building a multi-layered security framework encompassing asset reserves, storage management, risk protection, and public verification. Looking ahead, Gate will continue to uphold its security-first principle, further develop PoSEC standards and verification mechanisms, and collaborate with more industry participants to enhance asset security and transparency, laying a stronger security foundation for the long-term, sustainable development of the digital asset industry.

Learn more:

Gate, founded in 2013 by Dr. Han, is one of the world's leading cryptocurrency and integrated financial services platforms, spanning financial and everyday use cases including asset management, trading and payments. Serving over 62 million users globally, it supports trading across 5,400+ digital assets and 12,800+ stock assets and ETFs, while providing access to a comprehensive range of TradFi assets, including metals, stocks, indices, forex, and commodities to meet users' end-to-end needs across asset holding, trading, and spending. As an industry benchmark, Gate was among the first platforms to implement 100% Proof of Reserves. Its ecosystem includes Gate Money, Gate Wallet, Gate Ventures, Gate for AI Agent, and a wide range of products and services.

#9733. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

#9732. Browser-local image tools: how to check the upload boundary

This guide comes from the ImgIng project. It explains how to evaluate an image tool's processing path; it is not an independent security audit or a comparison of compression performance.

A browser interface does not tell you where a file is processed. A web app might run a codec on your device, send the source to a service, or combine both paths. The useful question is more specific than “is this website private?”: what does this selected operation send, receive, and save?

ImgIng's published documentation describes common image-processing routes as local to the browser. It also documents specialist-server exceptions. Reading an existing HEIC photo is a different operation from exporting a new HEIC file, for example. A local compression workflow does not establish that every conversion offered by the same site is local.

These are documented boundaries, not measurements performed for this post. Check the current tool notice because file type, output choice, and product changes can affect the route.

A local application still needs its page, scripts, and other assets. Some workflows also download a codec or a machine-learning model before processing can start. Network activity alone therefore does not prove that the source image left the device. Conversely, finding one local worker does not prove that another part of the workflow never sends data.

Squoosh provides another useful distinction: its official README describes local compression, while separately disclosing analytics. Local image processing and the absence of all telemetry are different claims. Evaluate each requirement separately.

Browser inspection can provide observations for a particular run; it is not a complete security audit. If your organization restricts uploads, follow those handling rules and verify the selected route before using confidential material.

For compression comparisons, retain the input and output files, actual byte sizes, dimensions, format, exposed quality settings, errors, and unsupported cases. Compare equivalent tasks: PNG-to-PNG optimization and converting PNG to WebP answer different questions. Smaller files can still lose detail or behave differently in the destination workflow.

The aim is a reproducible decision about a concrete job, with the data path and output quality evaluated independently. You can explore ImgIng using a permission-cleared example and the current operation notices.

Sources checked on November 6, 2026. Product statements are attributed to their publishers. No new compression benchmark, file-handling test, or security-audit result is presented here.

#9731. Inherited Green: Freeze Debt Accounting for Agent Patches

The conclusion first: an agent patch is not verified by the suite passing. It is verified by the assertions that executed in the head branch and did not execute in the base branch. Everything else is borrowed.

Most agent pipelines report one bit: green or red. That bit hides two inflators. Skips inherited from the base branch silently shrink the evidence surface. Property tests that re-draw their randomness on every run make a pass non-reproducible by default. Fix both and the patch review gets shorter, not longer.

This post is about accounting, not about catching flakes. Attribution work — deciding whether a patch caused a flake or merely surfaced one — is a separate gate. Here the question is narrower: how much of this green did the patch actually earn?

The following trace is illustrative, not a benchmark.

Nothing here is dishonest. The patch genuinely added two tests. The problem is that "+2" was reported without subtracting what the patch was already missing, and without noticing that the freeze covered the changed file.

So the rule is not "no skips". It is: skips are fine, unaccounted skips are not, and a skip whose blast radius overlaps your diff is a blocker unless a compensating check runs in the same build.

Add a session-level collector. It records executed and skipped node IDs with no plugin dependency, so it works the same in a container, a laptop, and a hosted runner.

Run it twice, in the same image digest, against the same dependency lockfile:

Same image matters more than it sounds. A drifted dependency between the two runs produces a delta that measures the environment, not the patch.

The script below answers four questions: how many tests net executed, what skips are new, what previously passed and no longer does, and whether the diff touches a frozen blast radius.

A positive net number is not a pass. It is a number that still has to survive the block list.

A freeze without a blast radius cannot be matched against a diff, and a freeze without an owner never ends. Fourteen days is a policy choice, not a measurement.

Three rules keep the ledger from rotting:

Property tests are the natural compensating check for a frozen example-based test. They are also the easiest way to produce a green that nobody can reproduce, because the generator picks new inputs each run.

When the hunting lane finds a counterexample, promote it: add a literal @example(Decimal("1234.56")) to the test. The pinned lane then replays it forever. A patch touching fee logic is expected to either add a promoted example or state why the invariant space did not grow. That is corpus growth as a reviewable artifact, not a coverage percentage.

Fixture changes are an evidence-surface change, not a code change. Diff them explicitly instead of relying on a reviewer to notice:

Any output triggers two requirements: human sign-off and a ledger entry with scope = "fixture". You do not need to judge whether the new fixture is weaker. You need it to be visible.

Numbers below are illustrative; thresholds are policy, not measurements.

This harness is deliberately boring to run: two pytest invocations in one image plus one script. The expensive part is the patch loop itself, not the accounting.

MonkeyCode's free model access keeps that loop cheap enough to generate candidate patches in volume, and its free server option is one way to run the agent session and both evidence runs in the same hosted environment rather than splitting base and head across a laptop and a CI runner. Both availability claims are operator-supplied: no quotas, model names, hardware, or duration are asserted here, and the harness below is equally valid with a local model or no agent at all.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

Do not adopt this if your suite is under roughly twenty tests, if you have no flake history to freeze against, or if your CI has no budget for a second lane. In those cases the ledger is ceremony and the delta is noise. For a small patch queue, a plain diff review is honest and faster.

Run the delta over your last twenty agent patches before adding any new tooling. The number that matters is not how many went green — it is how many the block list rejected, and whether you agreed with it.

Code in this article is a sketch: the collector and delta script are written against standard pytest hooks and git diff, but you should expect to adjust the git ref, the ledger path, and the settings profiles to your repository before relying on any exit code.

#9730. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9729. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9727. How to Serve an LLM with an OpenAI-Compatible API on a Dedicated GPU Server

Posted on Nov 6 • Originally published at leoservers.com

Running a large language model on your own hardware gives you control over deployment, inference resources, and API access. With an OpenAI-compatible API, your applications can talk to a self-hosted model using the same client libraries and request formats you may already use.

This post summarizes how to do it on a dedicated GPU server with vLLM, an open-source inference and serving engine. The full tutorial, with all commands and tables, is linked at the end.

One caveat: compatibility doesn't mean every OpenAI feature is available. Supported parameters depend on the inference engine and the model you deploy.

GPU memory is the key constraint. You need room for the model weights, runtime overhead, and the KV cache. A 16-bit model needs roughly two bytes per parameter for raw weights alone, and real usage is higher. Size your GPU from the model's documented requirements and your expected workload, not parameter count alone.

On Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04, with a working NVIDIA driver (check with nvidia-smi), create an isolated environment and install vLLM:

The tutorial uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as an example. Check that your GPU has enough VRAM before choosing a model.

Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps the API off the public network, which is a safer starting point.

Because the API is compatible, you only change the base_url:

To serve remote applications, put Nginx in front of vLLM, enable HTTPS, and restrict access with firewall rules. The --api-key option doesn't cover every endpoint on the HTTP server (the /invocations endpoint needs extra protection), so never expose an unrestricted inference endpoint to the public internet.

Watch GPU utilization, memory, temperature, power, request latency, and tokens per second with watch -n 2 nvidia-smi. If memory runs short, reduce context length, choose a smaller model, or use a supported quantization method.

The complete walkthrough, including parameter tables and a troubleshooting section, is on the Leo Servers tutorial page:

#9725. A Space Heater Is the Hardest Question You Can Ask a Smart Plug

The most dangerous product pairing in a smart home catalogue is also one of the most common: a 1,500-watt space heater and a smart plug sold as handling 15 amps. On paper the arithmetic works. In practice the heater sits at the plug's continuous load limit for hours at a time, and hours are what the rating was never about. Smart plugs fail on heaters not because the rating is a lie but because the rating answers a different question than the one a heater asks.

Electrical ratings for switching devices distinguish peak load from continuous load, and the difference is thermal. A relay contact passing 15 amps heats up. A kettle asks for 15 amps for three minutes, and the heat dissipates before it accumulates. A heater asks for 12 amps for six hours, and heat accumulates the whole time: the contact, the solder joints, the PCB traces, and the enclosure all climb toward a steady-state temperature that a short-cycle product never reaches.

Standards reflect this. Wiring rules derate continuous loads to 80 percent of a breaker's rating precisely because sustained current is harder than switched current. A plug rated 15 amps peak is, in that framing, a 12-amp continuous device at best, and a 1,500-watt heater on a 120-volt circuit draws 12.5 amps. The numbers meet exactly at the line, and the line is where thermal ageing lives.

The failure is not dramatic. The contact resistance rises as the contact material oxidizes and springs relax under thermal cycling. Higher resistance means more heat at the contact, which accelerates the oxidation, which raises the resistance again. The plug keeps working through the whole decline, which is what makes it dangerous: a plug that clicks and heats for a season, warms its own enclosure measurably, and one day stops conducting or worse does not.

The measurable warning signs exist for people who look. A plug body noticeably warm to the touch after an hour of heater duty. Discoloration around the socket. A relay click that has grown softer or occasionally fails to switch the load the first time. Any of these on heater duty is a replacement, not an observation.

The specifications that separate a heater-capable plug from a kettle-capable one are rarely the headline amperage. Continuous rating at ambient temperature, not just peak. Relay contact material and whether it is rated for high inrush and sustained resistive load. Thermal protection: a plug that measures its own temperature and cuts off at a threshold has a future; a plug that has no idea how hot it is does not. Enclosure material and its heat deflection point. Whether the manufacturer publishes a duty-cycle or derating curve, because a vendor who does has tested the question a heater asks.

Metering matters too, but differently than buyers assume. Energy monitoring does not make a plug safer; it makes the decline visible. A plug that reports its own power draw will show the heater drawing what the heater draws, and a sophisticated one can report temperature. For a load that fails by slowly cooking itself, telemetry is the difference between a scheduled swap and a surprise.

The heater problem has structural solutions worth preferring. A heater with its own thermostat and tip-over protection needs a dumb socket, not a smart one; the intelligence is already in the appliance. Hardwired heater control belongs on a switch or relay rated for the continuous load with headroom, ideally in the wall, where a failure is containable. Where scheduling is the goal, the schedule belongs in the heater if it has one, or in a device deliberately chosen for continuous duty.

If a smart plug must carry a heater, the selection rules are strict: continuous rating with margin, thermal cutoff, a name-brand contact specification, and a periodic inspection habit. Treat the plug as a wear item with a service life measured in heater-seasons, and replace it on schedule rather than on failure.

Small heaters change the arithmetic: a 600-watt oil radiator draws 5 amps, inside the continuous envelope of a decent plug with margin to spare. The rule is not that heaters and plugs never mix; it is that the mix needs continuous ratings, not peak ones. Decide from the wattage plate on the appliance, not the amperage on the plug's box, and leave headroom for the heater's own thermostat cycling.

The procurement questions are about sustained duty, not the amperage on the box. What the continuous rating is at realistic ambient temperatures. Whether the relay is specified for sustained resistive loads and what its electrical life is at that load. Whether the plug measures its own temperature and what it does at the limit. What derating the manufacturer publishes. What the failure mode has been in fleet deployments, if the vendor will say.

A plug family that answers these is designed for the loads people actually plug in. A family that quotes 15 amps and stops is designed for kettles and marketing. The difference is invisible on a 3-minute kettle boil and decides whether the same plug survives a winter on a heater, which is where the whole category quietly gets tested anyway.

#9724. FOC Vector Control in Vertical Robotics: Torque Ripple Suppression and Gravity-Compensated BLDC Drives

Most wheeled robotic platforms operate on horizontal planes where motor loads are symmetric and predictable. In vertical robotics, however, continuous downward gravitational acceleration creates severe torque asymmetries between upward climbing, downward braking, and lateral traversing cycles.

Traditional trapezoidal 6-step commutation generates significant torque ripple and mechanical vibration. When amplified against a thin glass pane, this vibration compromises negative suction stability and causes rapid track slippage. To achieve smooth surface adherence and precise velocity control, modern vertical platforms rely on Field-Oriented Control (FOC) algorithms executed on embedded ARM Cortex or specialized motor-control microcontrollers.

Field-Oriented Control (FOC) Implementation on Vertical Loads

Field-Oriented Control decomposes the stator currents of a 3-phase Brushless DC (BLDC) motor into two decoupled orthogonal vector components:

The Direct axis current (Id), controlling the magnetic flux linkage.

The Quadrature axis current (Iq), controlling the dynamic torque output.

By maintaining Id at zero and precisely modulating Iq via Clarke and Park transformations, the controller achieves smooth, maximum torque-per-ampere output. On a vertical glass pane, this continuous torque modulation minimizes micro-vibrations, ensuring the vacuum sealing lip remains completely flush against the surface at all times.

Sensorless Position Estimation vs. Magnetic Encoders

Determining rotor angle at zero or low speeds is critical when initiating a climb on steep glass:

Hall-effect sensors offer coarse 60-degree electrical resolution, which is insufficient for ultra-smooth low-speed positioning under heavy load.

Modern high-reliability platforms utilize high-resolution magnetic rotary encoders (such as 14-bit absolute angle sensors) communicating over SPI with the motor MCU.

In cost-optimized units utilizing sensorless architectures, microcontrollers deploy High-Frequency Injection (HFI) or sliding mode observers to extract rotor position from Back-EMF signals without requiring physical sensors in the harsh, humid cleaning chamber.

Asymmetric Drive Dynamics and Gravity Compensation

When traversing horizontally across a large glass pane, the upper and lower drive wheels experience radically different physical friction loads:

The lower wheel absorbs the full dynamic weight of the chassis plus tether tension.

The upper wheel tends to experience slight traction reduction due to chassis tilt.

The motion control loop integrates a real-time Gravity Compensation Vector derived from the 6-axis IMU:

Feed-forward torque offsets are calculated continuously at 1 kHz control loop frequencies.

If the optical surface encoder detects micro-slipping (a discrepancy between commanded rotor revolutions and actual displacement), the FOC loop immediately throttles Iq to recover traction before track decoupling occurs.

Evaluating motor drive stability requires continuous bench testing under variable friction coefficients, such as transition zones between dry glass, surfactant-treated glass, and framed edge silicone. Key hardware benchmarks include:

Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) in phase currents during abrupt vertical-to-horizontal trajectory switches.

Acoustic noise profiles and decibel ratings under heavy vacuum suction versus low-power traversal.

Real-world mechanical thermal dissipation across H-bridge MOSFETs during continuous 60-minute runs.

For comprehensive hardware teardowns, motor drive architecture comparisons, and empirical bench data across current commercial vertical robotics, explore the technical reports and motor performance datasets published at Window Robot Lab:https://windowrobotlab.com/

Are you implementing Field-Oriented Control (FOC) or sensorless BLDC drivers in your robotics projects? How do you handle torque ripple compensation under dynamic external loads? Share your controller schematics and algorithm insights in the comments below.

#9723. How Crypto Wallets Are Becoming More Than Just Wallets

At the beginning of Bitcoin, there was no such thing as a crypto wallet as we know it today. You had a full node, took care of complex private keys, and that was it. A lot has changed since then. Simpler and lighter apps appeared over the years, making it easier for users to manage their coins. But the evolution didn’t end there: now, crypto wallets are more than just wallets.

These versatile apps can do a lot of things beyond just storing funds, signing transactions, and sending payments. Of course, it always depends on the brand and network(s) involved, but we can find many interesting features to take advantage of in numerous crypto wallets. Let’s explore some of them.

Historically, people's "identity"—even in the digital realm—has always been assigned and managed by third parties (governments, corporations, etc.). However, the decentralized world offers an alternative through the self-sovereign identity (SSI) model. As the name implies, this is a form of identity or personal verification that can only be managed by the user who owns that identity.

In this way, very specific data can be shared only when necessary, rather than all personal information—for example, only age is verified, and the name is never revealed. Some crypto wallets can handle this type of digital ID already, in different ways. In an SSI setup, the wallet generally stores the credential and its cryptographic keys on the user's device. The issuer creates and signs the credential, while a decentralized network may store a DID (decentralized identifier), public key, credential schema, or revocation/status information that helps verify it.

When the user presents the credential, the recipient checks the issuer's signature and relevant on-chain data without needing the credential itself to be public. Examples of wallets that already have this feature include Dock Wallet, cheqd Wallet, Privado ID Wallet, and the Obyte Wallet. In the latter, you can verify your real name, your email, your GitHub account, your status as an accredited investor by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), and more.

All of this is done via chatbots integrated into the same wallet. Then, the information is stored in your wallet, and you can selectively share parts of that information with whoever you like.

You can't communicate directly with your transaction peers in every crypto wallet, but you can in some of them—and with end-to-end encryption, too. You can even send messages on-chain, if you want, and enjoy some easier chatbots here and there. Depending on the system, messages may travel through a peer-to-peer network and be read only by the intended recipient, and never by someone else.

As for more public on-chain messages that will last forever, this can be done even on Bitcoin, but it’s not exactly user-friendly there. The process often involves converting your message to hexadecimal code, finding specific wallets that support this function or advanced features inside wallets, and pasting that hex code into a designated field, sending a transaction without funds. In other crypto networks and wallets, it’s just a matter of writing whatever you want in a user-friendly menu, pressing “send,” and paying a small transaction fee.

Chatbots aren’t that common, but they can be welcome, especially for beginners. They can respond to commands or help users perform actions from a familiar chat interface. They can be related to Large-Language Models (LLMs) like Plug Wallet or KaleidoSwap, or simply follow ingrained instructions without the risks associated with AI, like the Obyte Wallet. In the latter one, you can enjoy all of these features: encrypted chat, user-friendly on-chain messages, and classic chatbots.

These days, it’s rare that your crypto wallet can’t interact with smart contracts and make programmable transactions. Smart contracts are small computer programs stored in a certain ledger and designed to carry out specific, pre-set rules. They can automate payments, exchanges, loans, bets, games, and many other applications.

In practice, when you’re inside a crypto wallet, the most you will typically see regarding a smart contract is the permission requested by a specific Dapp to connect to your address and, likely, use some of your funds. Unless you are a developer, you probably have little idea how to "read" one—let alone create one. Most wallets won’t show you this, either, but there are some of them with friendlier smart contracts.

Obyte is one of them. You can create conditional payments and smart contracts in human language inside the app, all of it without coding and via encrypted chat.

Besides, if you’re sending a transaction or interacting with a Dapp, you’ll be able to see a clear preview of the results and fees before pressing “Send” or “Pay.”

Remember the familiar routine of creating a new account for every website? Wallet-based authentication offers another route. With Sign-In with Ethereum (SIWE), for instance, a user can prove control of an account by signing a message. The signature happens inside the wallet, while the application verifies it. The standard was designed to give Ethereum accounts a consistent way to authenticate with services outside the network itself.

This can make one on-chain account useful across multiple applications. The address acts as a persistent identity that can be used across many Dapps, with the wallet handling the signature needed to prove control. Beyond MetaMask for Ethereum, other providers of this feature include Para and WalletConnect for multiple networks.

Beyond your own businesses, you can also contribute to your community and help shape the future of your favorite networks by participating in governance. On-chain governance lets token holders vote on proposals whose results can trigger changes to a network’s rules, parameters, treasury, or other functions. The voting process and its powers vary from one network to another, but the wallet can provide the place where users review proposals, connect their address, and cast a vote with their governance tokens.

The mechanics can be quite simple. A proposal appears in a governance interface, the wallet shows the vote and any required transaction, and the user confirms it by signing. Some systems use delegated voting, so users can assign their voting power to another address instead. In other cases, holding a specific token or meeting a balance requirement determines who can participate.

Examples include MetaMask supporting governance voting through compatible Dapps, Keplr providing governance features for Cosmos networks, and Obyte allowing users to participate in on-chain voting through its wallet and governance website.

In the end, the word “wallet” is starting to sound a little undersized for all of this. The same account can connect a person to applications, support communication, authenticate access, interact with programmable software, and even decide on the future of a network. A crypto wallet remains a place to manage digital assets, but its role can extend much further, and it'll likely continue to do so.

#9720. Your Free Server's Local Disk Is Not a Database: Five Persistence Myths and a Restart Probe

You deployed it. It worked. Then the instance restarted overnight.

Now your chat endpoint answers as if the conversation never happened. Was that disk supposed to hold your state?

This is a myth-busting FAQ about persistence on small, free-hosted apps. It ships with a restart probe you can run in about ten minutes. All code below is a template; I am not publishing measured results for your host.

The claim. fs.writeFile is durable, so a local JSON file is fine storage.

Why it feels true. It survives your process crashing. That is real.

What to check. Does the instance keep its disk across a restart? Across a rebuild? Those are different events. Ask your host explicitly, and reread the storage docs.

Corrected model. Local disk is scratch space with a marketing problem. Treat it as a cache you cannot trust.

The claim. If the disk survived last time, it will survive next time.

Why it feels true. You restarted the service and your files were still there.

What to check. A redeploy often builds a fresh image on a fresh machine. A restart may reuse the old one. Your test must name which event it exercised.

Corrected model. Restart, redeploy, and resize are three separate experiments. Run all three, or stop claiming durability.

The claim. Losing a warm cache is fine, because the cache warms itself.

Why it feels true. In steady traffic, yes, it does.

What to check. What happens on the first request after a cold start, with five hundred users arriving at once? That is a thundering herd, not a cache miss.

Corrected model. A cold cache is a load event. Budget for it, or gate the refill.

The claim. A sessions.json on disk is a fine interim solution.

Why it feels true. On a single instance, it is trivially simple and fast.

What to check. Restart the box while a user is mid-conversation. If the session vanishes, users see a forgotten session and a fresh greeting. They blame the model.

Corrected model. Local-file sessions are a single-instance lock-in. Fine for a demo, dishonest as a default.

The claim. I log every prompt and response to app.log, so I can debug later.

Why it feels true. The file exists, and it grows.

What to check. Restart, then look for the file. If it is gone, your audit trail had a lifetime measured in uptime.

Corrected model. A log on ephemeral disk is a debugging aid for the current boot, nothing more.

Stop asking "is it stored?" Start asking "where does it live, and what kills it?"

The rule I use: anything a user would notice missing goes in the bottom row. Everything else may live above it.

Here is the probe. Standard library only, no dependencies.

The one rule that makes or breaks this test. PROBE_LEDGER must point outside the instance. Put it on your laptop, in paste buffer output you capture, or in any store that does not die with the box. A ledger on the same disk proves nothing.

Three runs, three answers. Now you know which event eats your files. Do not guess.

If your app calls a model, the only record of what the model saw is the journal you wrote. Lose it, and you cannot explain a bad answer later.

So extend the probe. Log a prompt hash and a response hash per call, to the same external ledger.

Hashes keep the ledger small and avoid storing user text. You lose readability, and you gain the ability to prove a call happened. That trade is usually the right one for a prototype.

Why hash instead of skip? Because "the model gave a weird answer" is unfalsifiable without a record. Twelve hours after a restart, your log is gone and so is your argument.

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

This probe is cheap to run and cheaper to run repeatedly. That is where a free server option and free model access genuinely help: you can host the tiny probe app, drive it with real model calls, and repeat the restart cycle without a paid round trip each time.

What this does not give you: any promise about durability, uptime, or retention. Availability of a free tier says nothing about persistence. That is exactly why you probe.

If you want to run this loop yourself, the free server option on MonkeyCode is enough to start, as long as you bring your own off-box ledger.

Not "where did I write it?" Ask "what kills this, and have I watched it die?"

#9719. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.
